item.title: Deep dive: Fluids in sepsis
item.description:
A consultant-level look at sepsis fluid resuscitation. FEAST (2011) showed boluses can harm, and three adult trials of restrictive versus liberal fluid found no mortality difference: CLASSIC (2022, ICU septic shock), CLOVERS (2023, emergency department hypotension, stopped for futility) and ARISE FLUIDS (NEJM 2026, early vasopressors). ARISE FLUIDS did show less pulmonary oedema with the restrictive approach. Each of these trials enrolled patients who had already received fluid. For fluid choice, SMART was positive while BaSICS and PLUS were neutral. The Hammond 2022 and BEST-Living 2024 meta-analyses put the probability that balanced crystalloids reduce mortality at about 90 percent, with a harm signal in traumatic brain injury. ALBIOS, the German ARISS trial (stopped early) and the UK ABC-Sepsis feasibility trial found no survival benefit from albumin, and ALCAMIST is still recruiting. ANDROMEDA-SHOCK-2 found that a personalised protocol targeting capillary refill time beat usual care on a hierarchical outcome, mainly through shorter organ support. The guidelines differ. Surviving Sepsis 2026 still suggests at least 30 mL/kg in the first 3 hours (conditional, low certainty). ESICM 2025 suggests up to 30 mL/kg. NICE NG253 (November 2025) recommends 250 mL boluses up to 1 litre, then senior advice. The evidence for de-resuscitation is thin: the first version of GODIF stopped after 41 patients, and the main trial is ongoing.

Take-home points

  • The 30 mL/kg figure rests on low-certainty evidence. Surviving Sepsis 2026 says 'at least', ESICM 2025 says 'up to', and NICE NG253 says 250 mL boluses to 1 litre, then senior review. Reassess after every bolus.
  • Use balanced crystalloid by default (about 90 percent probability of a small mortality benefit), but use saline in traumatic brain injury.
  • After initial resuscitation, restrictive and liberal strategies have the same mortality (CLASSIC, CLOVERS, ARISE FLUIDS). Early noradrenaline, given peripherally if needed, is reasonable and led to less pulmonary oedema in ARISE FLUIDS.
  • Guide further fluid with capillary refill time and dynamic responsiveness tests such as passive leg raise or stroke volume response, not static CVP alone (ANDROMEDA-SHOCK-2, ESICM 2025).
  • Albumin is not first line (ALBIOS, ARISS, ABC-Sepsis). Consider de-resuscitation once the patient is stable, but the trial evidence is thin and GODIF is still running.

item.title: Deep dive: Aneurysmal subarachnoid haemorrhage on ICU
item.description:
A consultant-level tour of ICU management after aneurysmal subarachnoid haemorrhage. Oral nimodipine (British Aneurysm Nimodipine Trial, 1989) is still the only drug proven to improve outcome. Magnesium (MASH-2), simvastatin (STASH), ultra-early tranexamic acid (ULTRA) and clazosentan (CONSCIOUS-3 and REACT) were all neutral for functional outcome, even when clazosentan reduced vasospasm. The rescue therapies for delayed cerebral ischaemia rest on thin evidence. Induced hypertension has one underpowered trial (HIMALAIA, 41 patients). Endovascular rescue has one small phase 2 trial (IMCVS) with worse 6-month mRS. EARLYDRAIN (JAMA Neurology 2023) cut unfavourable outcome from 44.8% to 32.6%, but the 2026 ESO/EANS/ESMINT guideline pooled it and made no recommendation. The guidelines diverge most on TCD: NICE NG228 advises against it outside research, while AHA/ASA 2023 rates it reasonable. SAHaRA (NEJM 2025) found no benefit from liberal transfusion. Population case fatality has stayed at about a third for two decades. Observational data on withdrawal of treatment and on early invasive care for grade V patients point to a self-fulfilling prophecy.

Take-home points

  • Give oral nimodipine to everyone. If it drops the pressure, manage the hypotension (for example with a vasopressor) rather than stopping it, and only pause it if blood pressure swings are significant.
  • Aim for euvolaemia, not hypervolaemia. Treat natriuretic hyponatraemia (fludrocortisone or hydrocortisone is reasonable per AHA) and don't fluid restrict.
  • Magnesium, statins, clazosentan and pre-treatment tranexamic acid don't improve outcome. Treating vasospasm is not the same as treating the patient.
  • Induced hypertension, intra-arterial therapy/angioplasty and prophylactic lumbar drainage are reasonable but unproven. NICE, AHA/ASA and ESO differ on them, and on TCD.
  • Don't withdraw treatment early on admission grade alone. Treat hydrocephalus and reassess, because clinical improvement before aneurysm treatment strongly predicts a good outcome.

item.title: Deep dive: Severe traumatic brain injury on ICU
item.description:
A consultant-level look at severe TBI on ICU. BEST-TRIP (NEJM 2012) compared two treatment protocols rather than ICP monitoring versus none, and found no difference. DECRA (NEJM 2011) found early bifrontal craniectomy worse at 6 months, no longer significant at 12. RESCUEicp (NEJM 2016) found that last-tier craniectomy cut mortality (about 27 vs 49 percent at 6 months), but many of the extra survivors were vegetative or dependent at 24 months. OXY-TC (Lancet Neurol 2023) found no benefit from adding brain tissue oxygen to ICP-guided care. BOOST-3 has not reported; it is active, not recruiting, with primary completion estimated for November 2027. On transfusion, HEMOTION (NEJM 2024; threshold 10 vs 7 g/dL) was non-significant but favoured liberal, and TRAIN (JAMA 2024; 9 vs 7 g/dL, mixed acute brain injury) was positive. TRAIN's TBI-only secondary analysis (JAMA Netw Open, Sept 2026) had a fragility index of 1, and meta-analyses disagree. CRASH-3 (Lancet 2019) showed no benefit from tranexamic acid in severe TBI, yet NICE NG232 (2023) says to consider it for GCS 12 or less within 2 hours. BTF 4th edition (2016; ICP above 22, CPP 60-70) contrasts with the SIBICC consensus tiered algorithms (2019/2020). IMPACT and CRASH models predict outcomes for populations. Cohort data on withdrawal of life-sustaining treatment (Canadian 2011, CENTER-TBI 2021) and late recovery (TRACK-TBI 2021) show the risk of a self-fulfilling prophecy.

Take-home points

  • BEST-TRIP tested protocols, not the monitor: use ICP and escalate in tiers (SIBICC is expert consensus, not trial evidence).
  • Last-tier craniectomy (RESCUEicp) saves lives, but many extra survivors are vegetative or dependent; discuss this with families before surgery. Early bifrontal craniectomy for diffuse injury (DECRA) did not help.
  • Brain tissue oxygen-guided care is unproven: OXY-TC was neutral and BOOST-3 has not yet reported.
  • Lean towards a liberal transfusion threshold (around 9 g/dL), but the TBI-specific evidence is fragile (HEMOTION non-significant; TRAIN TBI fragility index 1).
  • Be cautious about early withdrawal of life-sustaining treatment: much TBI mortality follows withdrawal, practice varies widely between centres, and some patients recover late.

item.title: Deep dive: Temperature control after cardiac arrest
item.description:
Deep dive from the 2002 HACA and Bernard hypothermia trials through TTM (33 vs 36 degrees, 2013), HYPERION (non-shockable, 2019), TTM2 (2021, hypothermia vs actively fever-controlled normothermia, no difference in 6-month death, more arrhythmia with cooling), HACA-IHCA (underpowered, futile), the BOX duration trial (36 vs 72 h fever prevention) and ICECAP (JAMA 2026, longer cooling does not help, no normothermia arm). Covers the 2025 ERC-ESICM shift from targeted temperature management to temperature control with fever prevention (at or below 37.5 C for 36 to 72 h, feedback device, no cold-fluid prehospital cooling, no active rewarming of mild hypothermia), differences with the AHA, practical management, outcomes, and grey zones: shockable and non-shockable subgroups, in-hospital arrest, illness severity, and ongoing trials STEPCARE (TEMP-CARE), IH-TTM and R-CAST OHCA.

Take-home points

  • The question has changed from 'cool to 33' to 'have I prevented fever': target 37.5 C or below with continuous core temperature monitoring.
  • ERC-ESICM 2025 suggests preventing fever for 36 to 72 hours; the BOX trial found no difference between 36 and 72 hours of device-based fever prevention.
  • If a device is used, use one with feedback; whether devices beat simple measures is being tested in STEPCARE (TEMP-CARE).
  • Do not actively rewarm comatose patients who arrive mildly hypothermic (32-36 C), and do not use routine prehospital cold-fluid cooling.
  • Hypothermia is not proven dead in non-shockable, in-hospital or illness-severity subgroups, but there is no good evidence to chase it outside a trial.

item.title: Deep dive: Prolonged disorders of consciousness: diagnosis and assessment
item.description:
A consultant-level review of PDOC diagnosis. Clinical consensus misclassifies roughly four in ten patients labelled vegetative as minimally conscious (Schnakers 2009), and a single C R S R misdiagnoses about a third (Wannez 2017), so repeated structured assessment is the standard. Task-based f M R I and E E G studies (Monti 2010, Claassen 2019, Bodien 2024) show covert command following in a minority of behaviourally unresponsive patients (25 percent of 241 in Bodien), but these are research tools with a high false-negative rate. The A A N 2018 and E A N 2020 guidelines are more open to such tools than the R C P 2020 guideline, which restricts them to registered research. The episode covers the R C P pathway (specialist referral beyond 4 weeks, at least ten C R S R occasions over 2 to 3 weeks, re-evaluation at 6 and 12 months), amantadine in traumatic PDOC, prognosis by aetiology and the R C P chronic and permanent definitions, and briefly the Mental Capacity Act angle.

Take-home points

  • Do not rely on a single bedside look: use the C R S R repeatedly (R C P: at least ten occasions over two to three weeks) after excluding sedatives, seizures, hydrocephalus and metabolic causes.
  • Anyone still disordered beyond four weeks should be referred to a specialist PDOC unit; consider amantadine for traumatic cases at 4 to 16 weeks (A A N Level B).
  • Covert awareness is real (cognitive motor dissociation in 25 percent of non-responders in Bodien 2024) but f M R I and E E G paradigms are research tools; a negative result does not exclude awareness.
  • The R C P 2020 guideline and the E A N 2020 guideline give opposite advice on activation paradigms; know your local position and document practicable steps under the Mental Capacity Act.
  • Prognosis favours traumatic over non-traumatic aetiology and M C S over vegetative state; trajectory on serial C R S R matters more than the label.

item.title: Deep dive: Death by neurological criteria (brainstem death testing)
item.description:
The Academy of Medical Royal Colleges 2025 Code of Practice (in use from 1 January 2025) replaced the 2008 Code without changing the definition of death. Key changes: apnoea test start PaCO2 at least 5.3 kPa, minimum 5 minutes, end PaCO2 at least 8.0 kPa, rise at least 2.7 kPa, pH below 7.3; time of death is now the completion of the second set of clinical tests (or the point the final two doctors are satisfied if ancillary investigation follows) rather than the first set; core temperature at least 36 C; sodium 125 to 160 mmol/L; red-flag groups folded into preconditions; ancillary investigation required when full examination or apnoea test is impossible or confounders cannot be excluded (including decompressive craniectomy and therapeutic steroids); CT angiography is the UK consensus ancillary test of choice, whereas the 2023 AAN/AAP/CNS/SCCM guideline recommends against it and a 2025 Canadian prospective study found CTA and CT perfusion did not reach a 98 percent accuracy threshold. ECMO requirements are unchanged, with supplementary 2020 UK guidance awaiting update. UK (brainstem) and US (whole brain) formulations differ conceptually but the bedside examination is near identical; the WBDP 2020 and AAN 2023 documents are consensus, not trial evidence. Case law (Bland, Re M 2020, Dance 2022, Casey 2023, DT 2025 EWCOP, Barts v MC 2025) holds that a person is not dead in law until Code-compliant testing, that disputes about testing go to the Court of Protection on best interests, and that once death is properly established there is no best interests analysis. NHSBT reports neurological testing in potential donors fell to 63 percent in March 2025 from 72 percent the year before, with DCD now 62 percent of deceased donors.

Take-home points

  • Know the 2025 Code numbers: apnoea start PaCO2 at least 5.3 kPa, 5 minutes minimum, end at least 8.0 kPa with rise at least 2.7 kPa and pH below 7.3; core temperature at least 36 C; time of death is at completion of the second set.
  • Ancillary investigation is required in defined circumstances (incomplete examination or apnoea test, confounders such as residual sedation, craniectomy, therapeutic steroids); document why, and do not treat CT angiography as infallible given the UK consensus versus US guideline and Canadian data.
  • On ECMO the criteria are unchanged; plan sweep or CO2 titration for the apnoea test and sample sites (on VA-ECMO, left and right distal arterial gases) with supplementary guidance.
  • If a family objects to testing or the diagnosis, follow Code 6.69: talk early, offer the lay summary and observation of tests, seek legal advice within days. Until Code-compliant testing the person is not dead in law; disputes about testing in adults go to the Court of Protection on best interests.
  • Test promptly: neurological testing in potential donors fell to 63 percent in March 2025 and the CMOs wrote in February 2026 backing the Code.

item.title: Deep dive: Withdrawing CANH in prolonged disorders of consciousness after Re Y
item.description:
In An NHS Trust v Y (2018) the Supreme Court held that withdrawing clinically assisted nutrition and hydration from a patient with a prolonged disorder of consciousness does not need a court order where the Mental Capacity Act and professional guidance are followed and there is agreement. Kate and Tom go through who the decision-maker is, the process in the BMA/RCP 2018 CANH guidance and the RCP 2020 PDOC guidelines, what the independent second opinion must involve, and when a case is finely balanced or disputed enough that it must go to the Court of Protection (including the 2020 Vice President's guidance). They look at how later judgments have applied this: criticism of years of drift in GU, AB and XR, a case where the court ordered CANH to continue against medical advice (YD, 2025), and a 2026 Mid Yorkshire case. They finish with what it means for early decisions on ICU.

Take-home points

  • Re Y removed the mandatory court application, not the scrutiny: with the MCA followed, the guidance observed and agreement reached, no court order is needed.
  • A finely balanced decision, a difference of medical opinion or a lack of agreement means a prompt Court of Protection application.
  • The safeguard the Supreme Court relied on is a genuinely independent second opinion with its own examination.
  • Drift is the failure the courts keep criticising: continuing CANH by default is not neutral, and the giving has to be justified.
  • Start and document the values conversation on ICU; it becomes core evidence later.

item.title: Deep dive: ARDS phenotypes and personalised ventilation
item.description:
Kate and Tom ask whether ARDS can yet be treated as more than one disease. Secondary analyses of older trials found hyper- and hypo-inflammatory subphenotypes that differ in prognosis and may respond differently to fluids, PEEP and simvastatin. The prospective UK PHIND study shows they can be identified near the bedside within about an hour, and the UK PANTHER platform trial is now testing phenotype-guided treatment (no results yet). They also cover the 2024 global definition (a consensus statement), driving pressure and mechanical power as associations rather than proven targets, harm or no benefit from personalised PEEP strategies (ART, EPVent-2, LIVE, EITVent), proning (PROSEVA), the ACURASYS versus ROSE paralysis story, DEXA-ARDS and steroids, and EOLIA and ECMO, then where the ESICM 2023, ATS 2024 and FICM/ICS guidelines diverge.

Take-home points

  • Inflammatory subphenotypes are reproducible and prognostic, but treating by phenotype belongs in trials until PANTHER-type trials report.
  • Driving pressure and mechanical power are associations from observational and mediation analyses, not proven targets: use them as warning lights.
  • Avoid prolonged high-pressure recruitment (ART showed harm), and prone early and for 16 hours or more when P/F is below 150 mmHg.
  • Routine paralysis is where guidelines split most (ESICM against, ATS conditionally for early severe ARDS): use it selectively.
  • Talk to an ECMO centre early for EOLIA-type patients. Steroids are suggested by ATS 2024 but not addressed by ESICM 2023 or FICM/ICS.

item.title: Deep dive: Vasopressors in septic shock
item.description:
Consultant-level look at vasopressor decisions in septic shock, built around the 2026 Surviving Sepsis Campaign guidelines. Early noradrenaline (CENSER, CLOVERS) looks safe but has not been shown to reduce mortality. Observational data and the 2026 guideline support starting peripherally rather than waiting for a central line. VASST and the UK VANISH trial place vasopressin as a catecholamine-sparing add-on rather than a life-saver, and observational data link later vasopressin starts with higher mortality. ATHOS-3 and a small single-centre methylene blue trial show blood pressure gains without proven survival benefit. On MAP targets, SEPSISPAM, the UK 65 trial and Japan's OPTPRESS (stopped early for harm with the higher target) underpin the new suggestion of 60 to 65 mmHg in patients aged 65 or over. Terlipressin and selepressin don't help.

Take-home points

  • Early noradrenaline is safe but has not been shown to save lives.
  • Start vasopressors peripherally rather than delay for a central line.
  • Target a MAP of 65 mmHg, or 60 to 65 in patients aged 65 or over; higher targets have looked harmful.
  • Add vasopressin as the noradrenaline dose rises: it spares catecholamine but has not shown a survival benefit.
  • Angiotensin II and methylene blue are rescue options with weak evidence; avoid terlipressin.

item.title: Deep dive: Acute myocardial infarction in the ICU
item.description:
Kate and Tom cover what reaches the ICU after myocardial infarction: culprit-only PCI in cardiogenic shock (CULPRIT-SHOCK), the negative ECLS-SHOCK trial of early VA-ECMO, the positive but complication-heavy DanGer Shock trial of the microaxial pump, immediate versus delayed angiography after cardiac arrest (COACT, TOMAHAWK), type 2 MI and troponin interpretation, and perioperative myocardial injury (VISION, MANAGE).

Take-home points

  • Culprit-only PCI in infarct-related shock; no routine intra-aortic balloon pump.
  • Routine early VA-ECMO did not improve 30-day survival in ECLS-SHOCK and roughly doubled bleeding and vascular complications.
  • In DanGer Shock a microaxial pump improved survival in selected STEMI shock patients (not comatose after arrest) at the cost of more complications; involve the shock team early.
  • After arrest, ST elevation goes to the cath lab; stable patients without it can have delayed angiography.
  • Do not treat a type 2 troponin rise like a type 1 infarction: treat the cause.

item.title: Deep dive: Neuroprognostication after cardiac arrest
item.description:
Kate and Tom walk through the 2025 ERC-ESICM prognostication algorithm for comatose survivors of cardiac arrest: the wider entry point (motor score below 6 at 72 hours or later), the two-or-more rule for poor outcome, the new favourable indicators, why neurofilament light is not yet recommended, bias from self-fulfilling prophecy and early withdrawal, and the UK best-interests framework (MCA 2005, Aintree v James, Re Y, RCP PDOC guidance).

Take-home points

  • Wait until at least 72 hours, exclude confounders (sedation, relaxants, temperature, hypotension, sepsis, metabolic) and examine carefully.
  • Poor outcome is likely only with two or more concordant predictors; one alone is not enough.
  • Look for favourable signs too (motor score 4 or 5, normal NSE, continuous EEG, no MRI diffusion restriction); indeterminate means observe and reassess, because late awakening happens.
  • NSE needs serial samples (24, 48, 72 h) and care over haemolysis; the guideline does not recommend neurofilament light yet.
  • Prognosis informs a best-interests decision but does not make it; keep the prognosis and withdrawal conversations separate and document.

Key sources

  • ERC-ESICM guidelines 2025: post-resuscitation care (Nolan et al., Intensive Care Med 2025)

  • An NHS Trust v Y [2018] UKSC 46

item.title: 7 October 2026 (extended): PRESSURE, neuroprognosis in the Court of Protection, and an ICU-referral PFD
item.description:
Covers 30 September to 7 October 2026. Extended edition (about 45 minutes); replaces the earlier versions from today. Items first published before 30 September are marked as recent context.

  • MHRA: no new National Patient Safety Alerts, device safety notices or Drug Safety Update this week. The field safety notice list for 28 Sep to 2 Oct was not yet published. There was a minor leaflet defect for levetiracetam granules (EL(26)A/40). MHRA alerts
  • PRESSURE (JAMA, 28 Sep; recent context). 1,900 ventilated children in 23 paediatric ICUs: a permissive MAP target above the 5th centile meant 37.5% less vasoactive drug for a 3 mmHg difference in pressure. Primary outcome: probabilistic index 0.52 (0.49 to 0.54). Takeaway: less is not proven better, but more is not obviously better. Paper · ICCN commentary
  • SAFER (AJRCCM, 30 Sep). Pulse vs non-pulse methylprednisolone in acute exacerbation of IPF, n=100: no significant mortality difference, with very wide confidence intervals. Paper · PulmCrit on pulse steroids
  • A2B secondary analysis (Anaesthesia, 6 Oct). Patient-reported ICU experience was no better with alpha-2 agonist sedation than with propofol; only 29% of survivors responded. Paper
  • BJA editorial on the AGP list (2 Oct). Scotland has dropped its aerosol-generating procedure list and moved to risk-based "air transmission" categories. England still has the list. The authors sat on the guidance panels. Editorial
  • Videolaryngoscopy, VCISpain (Anaesthesia, 2 Oct). 5,302 intubations: even with an excellent view, about 6% of first attempts were difficult or failed. Document the blade, the view and how the tube was delivered. Paper
  • SGLT2 inhibitors before surgery. The 2026 AHA/ACC guideline reaffirms its 2024 advice to stop 3 to 4 days before. UK CPOC/JBDS guidance: omit them the day before and the day of surgery, longer with bowel prep, and check ketones. CPOC/JBDS
  • A Hospital Trust v MB [2026] EWCOP 32 (newly available). Withdrawal of ventilation after cardiac arrest. The evidence was framed on ERC/ESICM 2025 multimodal criteria, and the judgment explains why SSEP was not done. Judgment
  • Cardiff and Vale UHB v ST [2026] EWCOP 44 (30 Sep). NG feeding withdrawn despite the family's faith-based objection. Repeated tube removal was treated as evidence of her wishes. Judgment
  • Royal Berkshire NHS FT v BM [2026] EWCOP 50 (released 6 Oct). Surgery under GA was approved with a stepwise, last-resort restraint plan. Judgment
  • Prevention of Future Deaths reports. Ref 2026-0390 (South Wales Central, 30 Sep): ED overcrowding, and prescribed antibiotics never given. Ref 2026-0353 (Essex, 17 Sep; recent context): a dispute over ICU admission criteria delayed transfer. PFD reports
  • Townsend v Epsom and St Helier. The Supreme Court hearing is confirmed for 12 to 13 January 2027. UKSC
  • PARAMEDIC-3 Bayesian analysis (Resuscitation, 25 Sep; recent context). Intraosseous-first had about an 82% probability of worse 30-day survival, but any effect is probably modest; there was a 98% probability of worse ROSC. Stick with IV-first and IO as the fallback. Paper
  • Early PaO2 in acute brain injury (Neurocrit Care, 28 Sep; recent context). Lowest mortality at roughly 11-30 kPa (ICH), 13-25 kPa (SAH) and 13-21 kPa (ischaemic stroke); above about 40 kPa looks harmful. Observational. Paper
  • Brain-TTM (JCBFM, 2 Oct). In 34 patients, targeting brain temperature was no better than targeting systemic temperature; the brain ran about 0.3°C warmer during maintenance. Paper
  • Intra-operative hypotension and pneumonia (Anaesthesia, 2 Oct). Retrospective, 151,036 patients: relative falls from baseline predicted pneumonia better than absolute MAP thresholds, but the effect was small. Paper
  • Antibiotic timing by NEWS2 and shock (Lancet Respir Med; epub Aug, now in print). About 100,000 encounters: each hour of delay was associated with higher mortality with shock or NEWS2 of 7 or more, and not below 7. This supports the NEWS2-7 one-hour rule. Paper

Unchecked this week: full texts behind Cloudflare (JAMA, BJA, Wiley, JACC, BMC Critical Care, Springer ICM), so numbers come from abstracts. Also unchecked: the Critical Care Reviews site, 39 Essex, RCoA, FICM and CPOC. The JAMA editorial on PRESSURE was not read.
